classIntro.speaker: Kadam Kyle
classIntro.text:
I was going to say one thing — that I'll guide the offering meditation, actually based in a little section in the book, and this is for a few reasons. One is that that section is just best meditated on, so we save our time having to read it in class and then not meditating on it — we just meditate on it. Two is because it's effective. It's also just a beautiful offering practice. And then because it's the practice done in Nyungne, it's really nice for us to do that as our honorary Nyungne practice, since we don't have one here at this point.

In the good old days, yeah. Not since David's been around. Okay, so it's been a minute. Next year. It's on the calendar. So this is our Nyungne attempt — doing this little offering practice, because it's explicitly in Nyungne. Basically, you imagine that you're in this beautiful, crystalline space called a bathing chamber — just a beautiful, crystalline palace space, and all the Buddhas come in, and then you offer all these incredible offerings to them, and they experience lots of bliss. So it's a really, really nice visualization to do. You do it in Nyungne every session. So this is our honorary ode to it.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, Precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace, You, who love all beings without exception, are the source of happiness and goodness. And you guide us to a liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded hands I turn to you, supreme unchanging friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you. May all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore. Going for Refuge I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment, go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Generating Bodhichitta Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections, may I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. Four Immeasurables May everyone be happy. May everyone be free from misery. May no one ever be separated from their happiness. May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment. Visualizing the Field for Accumulating Merit In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni, surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars. Prayer of Seven Limbs With my body, speech, and mind, humbly I prostrate and make offerings both set out and imagined. I confess my wrong deeds from all time and rejoice in the virtues of all. Please stay until samsara ceases and turn the wheel of Dharma for us. I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment. Offering the Mandala The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers, The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon, Seen as a Buddha land and offered thus, May all beings enjoy such pure lands. The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred, and confusion, my friends, enemies, and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments — please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons. Prayer of the Stages of the Path The path begins with strong reliance On my kind teacher, source of all good; O bless me with this understanding To follow him with great devotion. This human life with all its freedoms, Exceedingly rare and most meaningful — O bless me with this understanding All day and night to seize its essence. My body, like a water bubble, Decays and dies so very quickly; After death come results of karma, Just like the shadow of a body. With this firm knowledge and remembrance Bless me to be extremely cautious, Always avoiding harmful actions And gathering abundant virtue. Samsara's pleasures are deceptive, Give no contentment, only torment; So please bless me to strive sincerely To gain the bliss of perfect freedom. O bless me so that from this pure thought Come great unfailing conscientiousness, To keep as my essential practice The Dharma's root, the Pratimoksha. Just like myself, all my kind mothers Are drowning in samsara's ocean; O so that I may soon release them, Bless me to train in bodhichitta. But I cannot become a Buddha By this alone without three ethics; So bless me with the strength to practise The Bodhisattva's ordination. By pacifying my distractions And analyzing perfect meanings, Bless me to quickly gain the union Of special insight and quiescence. When I become a pure container Through the common paths, bless me to enter The essence practice of good fortune, The supreme vehicle, the Tantra. The two attainments both depend on My sacred vows and my commitments; Bless me to understand this clearly And keep them at the cost of my life. By constant practice in four sessions, The way explained by holy teachers, O bless me to gain both the stages Which are the essence of the Tantras. May those who guide me on the good path And my companions all have long lives; Bless me to pacify completely All obstacles, outer and inner. May I always find perfect teachers And take delight in holy Dharma, Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly, And gain the state of Vajradhara. Receiving Blessings From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text:
Meditation on making offerings. First just remember what we want to offer up — something that we want to break our attachment to, or just something that would create the causes that we desire. And though we'll offer many different things, you can just weave this principal object into the practice. You can also remember that it's important to recall the benefits of making offerings — to imagine vastly filling the whole of space and that the holy beings accept it with great bliss and delight. And just feel what that bliss would be like.

[Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] Shantideva now describes an elaborate visualized ceremony in which twelve mentally transformed offerings are presented to the Buddhas. These are scented water for bathing the Buddhas, heavenly raiment, ornamental jewels, perfumed oils for anointing the Buddhas, flowers, incense, food, lamps, palaces, jewel parasols, music, and the prayer for a continuous rain of offerings. We should remember when performing the following visualization that the enlightened beings have no impurities of body or mind that need cleansing. From our own side, however, we need to abandon our impure form externally and the evils and obstructions of our mind internally in order to attain the pure state of a Buddha. Thus the cleansing and purification that we're about to perform is in fact for our own benefit.

[Reading:] First we should visualize the bathing room in which the purification is to take place. The floor sparkles with beautiful crystal and the atmosphere is pervaded by sweet-scented sandalwood. Four jeweled pillars adorned with gems and precious stones stand in the four directions, while from the ceiling are suspended two precious canopies decorated with pearls. In the center of the bathing room is a pool filled with wonderfully scented waters. From three directions, three steps sparkling with gems lead down into the pool. Just get some sense of this beautiful crystalline bathing chamber.

[Reading:] Having visualized this beautiful setting, we now invite all the Tathagatas and Bodhisattvas to come and bathe in this pool. As we see them arrive, we manifest many goddesses from our heart, one for each of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. These goddesses take the garments of the enlightened beings and the Bodhisattvas while others wash them with the pure scented waters held in beautiful jeweled vases, all to the accompaniment of music and song. Next we visualize the goddesses as drying these guests with towels made from soft and beautifully scented cloth. Then we offer fine robes of suitable colors and many jeweled ornaments to the magnificent superior beings — Samantabhadra, Manjughosha, Avalokiteshvara, and the others. Then as if polishing pure refined gold, we anoint the radiant bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas with rare perfume whose fragrance pervades thousands of millions of world systems.

[Reading:] After anointing their bodies in this way, we visualize these holy beings in the sky in front of us and send forth beautiful goddesses to them, each one holding a separate offering. To these glorious beings the goddesses present the following: garlands of beautiful and sweet-scented lotuses, mandaravas, upalas, and other exquisite flowers; clouds of incense with delicate fragrance; delicious food and drink; lamps arranged on golden lotus buds whose light dispels the dark ignorance of thousands of millions of world systems; and a most beautiful celestial palace made of pearls and precious gems. Inside this gorgeous palace there are transparent floors carpeted with beautiful flowers, while on the walls hang priceless pearls and gems. Throughout the celestial abode, beautiful goddesses sing joyful songs in praise of the Buddhas. Throughout the palace stand many beautifully shaped parasols vast in diameter with handles wrought in gold and rims adorned with many kinds of jewels. All these magnificent offerings vibrate with the sound of delightful music whose beautiful harmonies completely dispel even the traces of all beings' misery.

[Reading:] The final offering of this group is our own prayer that until samsara ends, a continual rain of flowers, incense, and precious jewels may fall upon the images and statues of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, upon holy Dharma, and upon the sacred reliquary monuments.

Then just guide ourselves for the remainder of the practice, emphasizing whatever aspect of making offerings resonates and feels important. Then in our own time we can just rejoice in our effort and gradually arise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Pass me the tissues. Great. Let's read Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life. Again, 1 to 18. Does anyone want to be the reader for today? Going once. Oh, Mary Ann, yep.

shantidevaReading.speaker: Mary Ann
shantidevaReading.text:
Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life, Chapter 2: Purifying Negativity

(1) To maintain this precious mind of bodhichitta,
I make excellent offerings to the oceans of good qualities —
The Buddhas, the stainless jewel of the holy Dharma,
And the assembly of Bodhisattvas.

(2) However many flowers and fruits there are,
And all the different types of medicine;
All the jewels there are in the world,
And all the pure, refreshing waters;

(3) Mountains of jewels, forest groves,
And quiet and joyful places;
Heavenly trees adorned with flowers,
And trees whose branches hang with delicious fruits;

(4) Scents that come from the celestial realms,
Incense, wish-granting trees and jewelled trees;
Harvests that need no cultivation,
And all ornaments that are suitable to be offered;

(5) Lakes and pools adorned with lotuses,
And the beautiful call of wild geese;
Everything that is unowned
Throughout all worlds as extensive as space —

(6) Holding these in my mind, I offer them well
To the supreme beings, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
O Compassionate Ones, holy objects of offering,
Think of me kindly and accept what I offer.

(7) Lacking merit, I am destitute
And have nothing else that I can offer;
Therefore, O Protectors, who think of the welfare of others,
Please accept these for my sake.

(8) Eternally I will offer all my bodies
To the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Out of respect, I will become your servant;
Please accept me, O Supreme Heroes.

(9) Being completely under your care,
I will benefit living beings with no fear of samsara.
I will purify my previous evils
And in future I will commit no more.

(10) Within this sweetly scented bathing chamber
With a clear and glistening crystal floor,
Majestic pillars ablaze with jewels,
And canopies of radiant pearls spread aloft;

(11) With many jewelled vases filled to the brim
With scented waters that steal the mind,
And to the accompaniment of music and song,
I offer ablution to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

(12) I dry their bodies with matchless cloths
That are immaculately clean and scented.
Then I offer to the holy beings
Fragrant garments in magnificent colours.

(13) With various excellent raiments, fine and smooth,
And a multitude of supreme ornaments,
I adorn Arya Samantabhadra,
Manjushri, Avalokiteshvara and all the others.

(14) Just like polishing pure, refined gold,
I anoint the radiant bodies of all the Able Ones
With supreme perfumes whose fragrance pervades
Every part of the three thousand worlds.

(15) To the Able Ones, the supreme objects of offering,
I offer all the beautiful, scented flowers —
Mandaras, upalas, lotuses and so forth —
And exquisite garlands, finely arranged.

(16) I offer them vast and fragrant clouds
Of supreme incense that steal the mind;
And I offer delicacies of the gods,
Together with a variety of food and drink.

(17) I also offer jewelled lamps
Arranged on golden lotuses;
And on polished ground sprinkled with scent
And scattered with beautiful flower petals,

(18) I offer to those with the nature of compassion
A celestial palace resounding with heavenly praise
And hung with beautiful pearls and jewelled ornaments
Whose infinite radiance illuminates space.

postReading.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postReading.text: We were working on overcoming our attachment and desire by making offerings. We're just also making offerings in general and doing whatever else we'd like to get up to. So does anyone have anything to report from the week, please? And you can remember my little speech I gave last week about data sharing, too. Yes, Anne, thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Anne
practiceReports.text:
Hello. I started a new kind of temp assignment this week. Many, many hours sort of wedged into a schedule that was already pretty full. So there were three things that I did that really helped.

One was making offerings to practice. I was checking with Dale a bit about this, but just imagining a vast expanse of, like, this beautiful digital calendar that spread out through infinite time that was completely empty. And just like, I'm like, oh man, all the time in the world to do whatever I want. And I just kept offering that to the Buddhas. And what it helped me realize is that feeling came from inside of me. I create that feeling, and I get to decide whether or not I have that feeling, right? And if I want to, I can stop whatever I'm doing and enjoy that feeling again and then give it away, because I have an infinite supply of that feeling. That was very helpful.

The second thing — I already let you know about, but I decided this job, the main reason I'm doing it is to practice the six perfections. So corporate life is very funny, and there are many opportunities to practice all the things. And I can't tell you, like, ten times a day I would see an opportunity to practice patience or remember emptiness or giving or whatever.

And the third thing I did that was so helpful is, like many people in here, I really upped my commitment to a more extensive meditation practice than I've ever done before. And I'm like, can I still do this while I work this extra job? And I'm like, I can if I put that first, right? Instead of trying to fit my meditation practice around it. And when I put that first, what it does is it reminds me this job just doesn't matter that much. It really doesn't. But actually acting in that way reminds me that that's the truth of the situation. And boy, can that help calm me down.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thanks so much. That was beautiful. All three points are just really helpful and inspiring. And Shantideva, throughout this text, uses this image of a warrior in battle — putting on the armor and rushing into battle. And that's kind of like what you did. It was very sweet. You had a plan, right? You had a Dharma plan. You put on your helmet, got your shield, your sword, your chain mail, and whatever else. And you charged into battle with Dharma. Not charged into battle and then was a fair-weather Dharma fan. Or calling for help after it all fell apart. It was like, no — you made a plan, and you went in there. Dharma first, right? And that's very inspiring. It's a good reminder for all of us. It's worth its effort to do the same in any new adventure that we step into. So thank you very much. It's lovely. Others, please. Ryan, yeah?

practiceReports.speaker: Ryan
practiceReports.text:
I have data from watching my mind, the weakest link. So I notice that I'm the most vulnerable in the evening time, like around 6 to whenever, until I fall asleep. And then when I am weak, vulnerable to desires, attachment — or easily, like, in the zone of scrolling, or watching YouTube random videos. And I don't know if it's physical tiredness, or if it's mental tiredness, if there's such a thing.

I noticed that last night specifically, I just watched for a few hours, and I'm afraid to go home tonight, because, like, oh, it's going to be evening, I'm going to be tired, and I'm going to be vulnerable again. So that is my data, and I wonder if you have some practical tips specifically for this — when you are tired and you easily... I see a lot of people have cravings at night, to go to the fridge. Mine is a little different — being vulnerable to delusions, different delusions.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text:
Yeah, no, it's a really nice thing to notice — like the when and the how the delusions get us. And it's different for everyone. But this sort of nighttime space, especially tired nighttime space, is somewhere really tip-top on the leaderboard for delusion breeding ground. It's incredibly common. I think it's somewhat universal. Definitely tiredness, but just that nighttime tiredness, definitely.

Sometimes we just feel like, I owe myself a little delusion time. I've been so virtuous today, I need to create the causes of suffering. I'm going to make myself suffer. I was too positive today. These little funny things that we do — but part of it is that there's a tension that builds up throughout the day, and then it snaps. This happens to kids a lot. They're, quote-unquote, so good throughout the day, maybe at school or this or that, and they're holding it in and holding it in and holding it in, and then boom, snap. And usually it's the parents at night that get that little surprise for them, a little treat for them. So this is like a tension debt or relaxation debt. It's accrued throughout the day because we're tense, and at some point there's a critical mass of it where we just snap and then follow it.

So anyway, what to do about it. One: try not to accrue the debt throughout the day. We'll just practice Dharma. That's how. Two: get better at literally going to sleep when we're tired — not entertaining ourselves or distracting ourselves when we're tired, because distracting yourself isn't actually relaxing. It's agitating. So if we're actually tired, it's a really good practice to just go to bed. It doesn't matter what time it is. It doesn't matter if it's 6 p.m. Just go to bed.

Three: rotate the rhythm and routine. A lot of our delusions actually feed on certain rhythms and routines, and if you break them, they don't trigger in the same way. Delusions are very dumb. They're just ignorant minds. So often they're not even smart enough to rejig if we mess up their normal playing field. So what you'll probably notice is you have the same routine that at some point culminates in the delusion settling in and taking over. And you'll notice this is an exact pattern. This, then this, then this, and then they set in. So it's like, okay, can I do a different pattern? Can I have a different routine? Can I bring in — and this is just examples — can I bring in a nighttime walk? At seven or eight or whatever, I go outside with no device, and I contemplate my favorite little Dharma idea. I say some mantras as I walk around. Just break the rhythm completely. Or instead of sitting in that bed or on that couch, I sit at the dinner table. And I have a little book there, no device. And I just have a slightly different routine. Or maybe I save a bunch of my cleaning and my work and whatever for that time period — so instead of it being delusion time, I do a bunch of things that aren't taxing but I have to get done anyway. That I don't actually want to do when I'm fresh in the first place. Save my fresh time for more fun things, like meditation. And have a little to-do list. This is what I do at night. I'm going to do my cleaning, my organizing, get my clothes ready for the next day, do my shower, and so on. All my routine. It's just ideas, but the point is about changing the habits, the patterns. Our mind is just pattern-based. It just follows the patterns. So you just break the pattern, and often delusion will get confused, at least. It will be slowed down.

Anyway, those are a few ideas. I think that will be a good start. And it's nice — you noticed it. You're aware of it. That's the biggest part of this sort of practice. Thanks. Others, please. Mimi, yes.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text:
Okay, so this is what happened, and this is how I practiced. So I was in Fayetteville last week. And what came up for me was really thinking and contemplating on the Three Jewels — Sangha, Dharma, Buddha. And what I noticed was that being in my home with my biological family, who I love and adore and love being there — but I felt closer to my spiritual family. Maybe it's because I spend more time with you all. Maybe because you know my intimate thoughts, because I practice. I just felt this real vivid connection to my spiritual Sangha, my spiritual family.

Then with Dharma, I noticed that I'm practicing and living the Dharma, and that it was in sharp contrast with my family, who don't. And I could see this difference. Not in a judgmental way, just noticing. And then with Buddha, my home is imbued with Buddha. My shrine — I have Buddha images on the fridge, on the door, Geshe-la's all around the house. It's just like Juliana and I live in this space filled with Buddha. And in my mother's home, even though she's Catholic, there's religious images, but there wasn't this feeling of Buddha being there. So it was really interesting.

So what came up for me was really thinking about my own karma — how I really thought about this previous self that helped me meet Kadampa Dharma. I haven't followed any other Dharma, any other teachings. It's just Geshe-la's teachings from the very beginning. And I thought about refuge, going for refuge. And I thought about my reliance on the spiritual guide. So those things really came up for me during this visit.

And so what did I do? My family is connected to the Dharma through me, right? But I did Heart Jewel. And I just sat in the dining room in the early morning, or in my dad's office in the early morning, and I really asked Dorje Shugden to come. And I asked the Shugdens, the four Shugdens, to be guardians all around the garden, and to protect my mother, and protect my brother, and my family. I just really prayed. I was like, this home is devoid of the Buddhas, you know? And that's my data.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thank you, Mimi. Yeah, it all makes a lot of sense. The only thing, just from my side, is — I don't know if you had a little travel shrine with you, but that goes a long way. And it took me a while to fully embrace the travel shrine, because it just felt a little bit awkward, and I didn't want to travel with my Buddhas and break something or disrespect them. Just as a little extra step, a little bit of laziness would creep in. But I found that when I travel somewhere and I have a little travel shrine, it makes a gigantic difference in the actual physical space. And you feel like you're with the Buddhas, and you have your own little corner. It's just a little tiny corner, maybe, of wherever we've gone. But it makes a magnificent difference. And it's really worth it. You just make a little kit. Just like we have a little toiletries kit, you just make a little travel Buddha kit. Tarpa has one, and it's great. That one's fantastic. But you can just make your own too. You just get a Buddha card, a little Dharma card, and then a little stupa. Then you've got your shrine, and then one little offering, like a little bowl with some water that you put in it each day, or a little flower, or a little gem. It can almost fit in a wallet, basically, what we're talking here. But it's an incredibly practical thing to do. Very smart. Very practical. Yeah, thank you. Others, please. Fran, yes, thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Fran
practiceReports.text:
I've got a couple of data points that both involve banishing delusions and unnecessary things. I'll try to make it succinct. Last week during discussion, Adriana and I were talking about — I was talking about my Heart Jewel practice and how I have trouble getting started with it in the morning. I enjoy my cup of coffee with my crossword puzzle, whatever, and it's almost like a reward to myself. That's my time, too, before my day gets very busy. And Adriana said, you have to banish the games. And she was right, and I did.

It made a tremendous difference to let go of the attachment and to do my Heart Jewel practice first thing in the morning, and to do my Lamrim practice first thing in the morning. And my days were lighter and easier. I didn't feel like, oh, I have this Dharma commitment, this meditation commitment that I have to do. Where am I going to squeeze it in? Where am I going to fit it in? And I still got my successions done, and I've really been doing reading, and the Lamrim — I've been embracing it. I totally forgot the offering part of this week, but it's in there. It was involved in there.

And what I've done with my Lamrim practice that I've found very helpful is I committed to memorizing the order of the Lamrim, which helps me when I sit down to do my Lamrim meditation to sort of build up the steps to where I need to be at that moment.

So the other banishing was — even with all that, I still have a problem with discouragement, and with not feeling good enough, and it's not enough, and I need to do more, et cetera, in a lot of aspects of my life. And with the help of Kadam Kyle, I was able to identify that that's the delusion of discouragement, and that it's laziness of discouragement — avoiding things that I don't want to do and not getting them done. So after talking about it for a while, we decided I was going to put a face on it. And I created — and it's still in the process of creation, of making it even more scary — a demon for myself, that when I say, oh, I should be doing that, no, I'll do it later, up pops this demon that's threatening me. And he's big and scary, hands up, big teeth. And having that face on it, I realized that all I have to do is bop him on the face, and he turns around, and he cowers, and he runs away. So it's just acknowledging him: you're not going to hurt me. And what's happened that's been really pleasurable is sometimes when I'm dealing with this delusion, this demon, Dorje Shugden then appears next to me on his snow lion and helps me scare him away.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Thank you. Banish the games, and bop discouragement on the head. It's lovely. I love that. This is what we often do, this practice of anthropomorphizing a delusion, because it makes it different than us so clearly, and then we view it as an enemy and distance ourselves in that way. Yeah, thank you. We're looking forward to the image, if you ever get it. Or Juliana, too. She could do a good anime version of it. Others? Adriana, yeah? Thanks.

practiceReports.speaker: Adriana
practiceReports.text:
The suggestion that you made about there being something magical about offering in 3D — I know that being a Vajrayogini practitioner, I've tried to offer and transform, purify and transform attachment into offerings to myself as a future Vajrayogini, and it really didn't make sense, and it felt awkward or forced. But there is something inexplicably magical about the three-dimensional island that you suggested.

So I have two islands. I have Jewel Island and Fabric Island. So on Jewel Island, it's all these beautiful crystal palaces and towers, and that's where my attachment to admiration and praise and reputation — they live on that island. And then the other island is all the beautiful furniture and clothing in the world. So I feel so good about these islands. There's something very tangible that I'm offering. It's like, here, you guys, go crazy. Like, really enjoy it. And the Buddhas have a lot of fun on my islands.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text:
Yeah, thanks. It's a good teaching about some Dharma practices. When something's not connecting, it's tempting to do it less, but in this case, it's actually do it more. There's a lot of things that are like that. Like the succession guru yoga for me is like that. When I did it at the bare minimum, I would do it, but I'd check a box. But then I got advice at some point: just do it longer then. And when I did it longer, I loved it. And then I looked forward to it every day. There's a lot of little practices like this. Visualization is definitely one of those. If we do it really 2D and half-hearted, it's just hard for it to be inspiring. But if you make it alive — there's something that clicks. If you get a little indulgent with it, something clicks that makes it incredibly lovely and beautiful. And you want to be in it. So sometimes — sometimes we do need less of something. If we're feeling overwhelmed and discouraged, we need to tone it down. But sometimes actually we need more. Because we need to give ourselves a little space to find the delight in it. And anyway, it's nice that you could do that. The practice of putting our practice into the island is explained in Great Treasury of Merit. Yeah, thank you.

Okay, let's take a look at the text. Thank you all. All right, so we are on to Offering our own body. Page 66.

[Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] In all my lifetimes I will offer all my bodies to the Buddhas and their Sons. Please accept me, O Supreme Heroes, as I reverently become your subject and follow your advice. Protected by your power, I will remain unafraid of the sufferings of samsara and will benefit others. My previous evils will be purified, and in the future I will commit no more.

[Reading:] By offering our own body to the enlightened beings, we can accumulate great merit. We will gradually purify the effects of our past non-virtuous actions and refrain from committing further misdeeds in the future. Why is this? The immeasurable non-virtue we have committed since time without beginning has been the fault of our self-cherishing attitude. With a selfish attitude toward our own body, we have engaged in innumerable negative actions, trying to get the best for ourselves at all costs. Therefore, if we are able to offer our body to the enlightened beings, thereby depriving our self-cherishing attitude of its chief object, there will no longer be any reason to commit non-virtuous actions. If we can overcome selfishness and miserliness by mentally offering ourselves as a servant to the Buddhas, we will experience many positive results. Moreover, by constantly meditating in this fashion, we are preparing ourselves to offer our actual body as a servant. The unsurpassed benefits of this action are evident in the life of the great Milarepa, who surrendered his body as a servant to his teacher, Marpa, and as a result of his intense guru-devotion attained full enlightenment within one lifetime.

[Reading:] If we offer not only our present body but also those of our future lives to the Buddhas, we will be free from the fears of samsara. When a person offers himself and his services to a king, he receives royal protection, and as a result no one dares to harm him. In a similar fashion, if we offer our body to the Buddhas, it becomes their servant, and is beyond the harm caused by human and non-human beings alike.

This last little bit reminds me of the warnings on the trains, like if you assault an MTA worker, you're basically locked up until the end of time. It's like they have royal protection from the city. They're not just normal people anymore. I don't know what happened that led to that fine being established, or those threats being established, but obviously they're getting beat up a lot and harassed a lot. So they have royal protection — no one even dares mess with them, except in Rockaway. So it's a little bit like that. Or it's like being the errand person for a mobster. You're at the bottom of the barrel, but no one's going to mess with you, because you're connected to the mob. King is just a big mobster. They're just an institutionalized mobster. So it's the same thing.

So this practice is incredible, and it's everything. Because this practice is about overcoming self-cherishing, which is everything. Where to start? We of course need to have a fear of continuing to identify and cherish this body as ourself. So we need to have a fear of that. It's not a fear of sickness, it's not a fear of death, it's not a fear of someone not liking us, or something bad happening, or of pain. It's a fear of cherishing this body as ourself. That's what we want to fear. Which basically means feeling it's dangerous to do that. It's dangerous to keep thinking of this body as myself.

When we encounter a lot of sickness and pain, we know in that moment: if only I didn't think of this body as myself. Because it hurts so bad right now. It's so awful to deal with right now. It's betraying me. If only I didn't think of it as myself, then I would be free right now. This would be no problem. If I saw it as my car, I wouldn't be having these kind of problems anymore. Your car can have serious issues, and be dented and broken, whatever — but you don't hurt in the same way. Because we don't think, I am my car. But when we think, I am my body, we cherish our body as ourself. It's unbearable when it's in pain, when it has problems. It's also implying identifying our delusions as ourself, and our ordinary mind as ourself here. But we can just think "body" for the time being. Because that's the main object of our self-cherishing.

So this is the first thing to make this practice work. We want to feel like it's dangerous to think I on an ordinary suffering body and mind. What if we get nerve pain that sets in, that never leaves us until we die? Like today. That could happen very easily. There's just one day that that happens. You get pains like that. It's not like you get a warning. So if that happened today for us, and we're thinking of it as I, how would we do? We'd probably be frantic. Oh my gosh, I have to make this stop. We'll start Googling and talking to our little AI friends for help. Help me, please. Go to the doctor, go to the emergency room. We're frantic, trying to find answers. That can happen at any moment. As long as we think of this as ourself, we're in big trouble. What about all the different cancers and diseases that are going to set in in this body? This body is just a cesspool for disease. It's a disease magnet. It's a pain magnet, actually. The fact that we have little nerves everywhere in our body, ready to get triggered at any moment. It's a pain magnet, this thing. And the machinery breaks down, as we all know. And as it breaks down, we become helpless.

So the point is, we want to develop this sense — basically, having the mind of self-cherishing is dangerous. Just like a scary enemy is dangerous, or war is dangerous, the mind of self-cherishing is actually more dangerous than any of these things. It's much more dangerous. Then, on the basis of that, we're going to develop a thought: I want to exorcise this demon of self-cherishing from my mind. It's a little bit like Fran's example earlier of imagining discouragement as a demon or a Mara. We want to have that same feeling. I want to exorcise self-cherishing from my mind, this demon of self-cherishing. It's dangerous. I want to remove it from my mind.

I had shared this earlier, but I'll share it again, because it was a great teaching for me. When I drove in today, there was a car flipped on its side on Atlantic Avenue, and another car smashed into a dumpster. There was a mother and a child in the car flipped over, and they were banging on it to get out, trying to escape, but they couldn't escape because they were pinned to the ground, in glass, right in the middle of Atlantic Avenue. I walked over to check what was going on, because the ambulances hadn't gotten there, and seeing them wriggle and try to escape was very powerful. That sense of urgency. Like, I need to get out. I would be thinking, if it's going to explode, or just get hit by someone else, because you're just in the middle of the road, strewn in there. You're with your child. Anyway, it was very powerful, and thankfully firefighters came, and they got them out and helped them escape. Somewhat worked out.

But it was a fantastic image, right? What would it be like for me, when I wake up in the morning and I see my self-cherishing mind or my self-grasping mind, to have that same sense of urgency? Obviously, their version is a bit neurotic and fearful — we're not talking about a neurotic feeling here, but that same sense of drive is the same. That drive is the same. Like, I need to do this. This is important for me. That kind of mind, that part is the same. Wishing to get rid of self-cherishing and self-grasping is completely peaceful. That's the difference. Wishing to get out of a car so you don't get crushed or explode isn't very peaceful. But the drive is the same, that sense of urgency.

When we think of self-cherishing, we start seeing the mind as dangerous. That's step one. Step two: we develop this sense of urgency and strong interest. I need to exorcise this mind. For my safety, really. So I can be safe. So I can be protected. I'm not safe, basically, until I have exorcised the self-cherishing mind. And then step three: we start opposing it in different ways.

There's all sorts of things we can do. One of the simplest is to offer our body in the sense of serving the Dharma center, helping the Dharma center, helping Dharma flourish. This is a great practice. It creates all sorts of mind-boggling merit. But it's a way to practically offer our body, just in service. This doesn't mean do things for the Dharma center. It means with a mind of offering our body as a servant to all the Buddhas, do things for the Dharma center. Those are two different things. Because you can do things for the Dharma center without a mind of offering — out of guilt, out of pressure, out of a sense of coercion, a sense of boredom. So that's not the practice. The practice is thinking, I want to offer my body. I want to break my self-cherishing mind down. So I'm going to offer my body to the Buddhas through helping Dharma flourish. So that's one of our important practices. So it's nice to have a little job or two at the Dharma center.

Second thing to do — we're not going to get to all of what we're going to do, we'll do more of this in the second session. To start, just remembering that I and the label I and this body are not the same. This is a very, very important practice. Basically, we're trying to tell the difference between what's called the basis of imputation and the imputed object within the name. It's very hard to oppose self-cherishing if we think, for example, the body and the I are one. It's a bit complicated, right? Because you just think, well, that's me. So how do I stop caring about that label I? One of the easiest things to do is to start seeing I and the body are not the same. I is just a name put on the body. The body is not the self.

I don't know if you've ever read this section in the View of the Transitory Collection, in How to Understand the Mind. This is an incredible section. I was just very blessed — one of my side hustles is grading the International Teacher Training Program exams, which I love doing. I feel very honored to do. So I graded 170 answers to this section. This is one of my three questions I had to grade. The View of the Transitory Collection is incredibly inspiring. The answers were amazing. It was all the resident teachers' exams, and they were amazing. A lot of it was not necessarily verbatim, but extensively thorough and very inspiring. So I got to read this section 170 times yesterday as one of my activities. And there are some things in here that are not in any other book. It's emptiness teaching. It's 12 or 13 pages. It's a little emptiness teaching. It's very unique and beautiful and really worth our time and energy to read. Just for fun, really. Just sit and relax with a cup of tea or coffee and just read it. Let it touch your heart.

I'm just going to read one little part because it related to the car accident. [Reading from How to Understand the Mind:] Suppose a child is named Buddha by his parents. The child would grow up thinking, I am Buddha. But when he discovered that Buddha was someone who was free from the two obstructions, he would examine his body and mind and realize that he was not an actual Buddha, but just an ordinary person with the name Buddha. Although he might continue to call himself Buddha, he would know that this was merely a name and that did not imply that he was actually a Buddha. Our situation is similar in that we have always thought of ourselves as I and assumed that corresponding to this name, there was a real I. We search for this I and will not find it, either within our body and mind or outside ourself, and we will realize I is just a name. Just like the name Buddha. Behind this I, there is nothing at all.

So when the accident happened, this man came running up, and I was very curious. I thought he was concerned about the accident, and he told me, no, last week another car flipped here, and I was parked over here, and I was afraid, so I came to check on my car, and her name is Jenny. He said, I was just really concerned about Jenny. He was pointing out the SUV. And I was like, you just love Jenny, don't you? And he's like, yeah, I just love Jenny. And it was just a great teaching. It was teaching this exact point. There's no Jenny, right? But the second you put that name, it starts to feel like there's something there. But it's just a name, just a word. And so Buddha is saying, that's the same with I. It's no different than Jenny on the SUV. That's it — just a name. So I is not the body.

We'll do more in the next session. But that was a good start. Feeling it was dangerous to have self-cherishing, developing a strong urgency to abandon, banish, exorcise self-cherishing, and then we can start working on it by giving our body to flourishing Dharma with that intention, and then remembering I is not the body, just a name.

Okay, good. So let's dedicate here. We can just close our eyes. We can think through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing. May all living beings find lasting peace of mind and enlightenment. We can make any personal dedications. Okay, thank you. Thanks, everyone. So we'll come back at 6 o'clock.

chantedPrayers.text: Liberating Prayer O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha, Precious Treasury of Compassion, Bestower of Supreme Inner Peace, You, who love all beings without exception, are the source of happiness and goodness. And you guide us to a liberating path. Your body is a wish-fulfilling jewel, your speech is supreme purifying nectar, and your mind is refuge for all living beings. With folded hands I turn to you, supreme unchanging friend. I request from the depths of my heart, please give me the light of your wisdom to dispel the darkness of my mind and to heal my mental continuum. Please nourish me with your goodness that I in turn may nourish all beings with an unceasing banquet of delight through your compassionate intention, your blessings and virtuous deeds, and my strong wish to rely upon you. May all suffering quickly cease and all happiness and joy be fulfilled and may holy Dharma flourish forevermore.
chantedPrayers.note: Only the Liberating Prayer portion of Session 2 prayers was captured in the transcript.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
I would like to feel a real sense of urgency to stop thinking I on this ordinary body and mind. Let's see if we can get a mental image of what this would feel like and be like. I'm going to stay with that for the final couple of minutes. And then in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

Okay, so a little bit more on offering our body. We're now going to mostly focus on self-cherishing. I wonder if anyone has a handy definition of self-cherishing for us. What precisely is self-cherishing? Mary Ann, yeah?

Yeah, that's pretty good. The attention given to self while regarding it as real, while neglecting others. Yeah, that's getting in the ballpark. Anne, you have one, yeah? Regarding myself as more important than others. Yeah, regarding oneself as more important than others. To some degree, that's a sort of colloquial use of it, but it's not quite the precise thing that we're going for. If we're just teaching a class or something and quickly explaining, then that's correct. But I'm looking for a definition. Let me just read from New Eight Steps. It's pretty close to what Mary Ann said.

[Reading from New Eight Steps to Happiness, page 90:] What exactly is self-cherishing? Self-cherishing is our mind thinking "I am important" while neglecting others. It is defined as a mind that considers oneself to be supremely important and precious, and that develops from the appearance of true existence of the self.

So the bit about "and develops from the appearance of true existence of the self" is an important part of that. Because if you're imputing self on Heruka, not other than emptiness, you can think that person is incredibly important. There's nothing wrong with thinking Heruka is important. The problem is thinking I on an inherently existent body and mind, and thinking that's important. So it's not just self that's the object of self-cherishing — it's a self that's developing from the appearance of true existence of an I or self. That's the object of self-cherishing.

And then "considers oneself to be supremely important and precious" — we can use this combo, which means it's thinking I'm important, and it's also neglecting others. That word "neglecting" is really important here. It's a key bit.

I personally have found it very useful to think: how has my self-cherishing made me neglect others? And who have I neglected because of my self-cherishing? This is an activity that we've maybe done in our life in a way that makes us feel guilty and ashamed, but that's not what we're talking about here. We're talking about an activity that helps us really hate self-cherishing. Not ourselves, not other people, not blaming ourselves — but we're really starting to dislike self-cherishing profoundly. We're thinking, who has self-cherishing made me neglect? And it's really nice to have a list of people, and to run through them occasionally, and just go: self-cherishing made me let this person down. Self-cherishing made me not able to help this person. Self-cherishing made me turn my back on that person.

It's a very powerful force to do this activity. So again, we're not doing it out of guilt — guilt saying, I let them down, I turned my back on them, and not understanding it's the delusion that basically forced us to do that. It's the delusion's fault. We're doing this exercise to really want to exorcise the self-cherishing mind completely. So I have my list, and I personally find it very grounding to do this activity. It gets my mind out of the sky and just back into reality. I was thinking about this guy Dan that I knew in New England — and I feel like, oh, my self-cherishing mind let him down. I just saw a picture of him recently on social media. Wow, it really made me betray him. Not in an overt way, but just not be there for him in the way I wish I could have been. It's very grounding. Like, thank you, okay. I'm going to get this mind out of here. I don't want to have another person like that. I don't want to have that effect on this person and that person.

This is useful because also, whenever we're practicing Dharma, there are things that we try not to do out of delusions, but then we end up not doing them out of virtues either. So I'll give an example: caring what people think. At first, either we're completely callous and don't care at all, and then we need to train in caring what people think. But a lot of people who get into Dharma, at least in New York City, care what people think coming from a delusion. So they come to a class, and they learn, you don't need to care about what people think about you from a delusion. Basically, you don't need to follow the attachment that wants to be liked. But you should care what people think about you from consideration for others, which is a virtue. It's a virtuous mind that basically controls our actions on behalf of others. It deeply cares what people think, but it's coming from a virtue.

So you could hear a teaching, "don't care about what people think about you," and what it means is don't do that coming from a delusion, of course. But that doesn't mean don't do that coming from a virtue. It's not the same activity. Or people run into this issue when they learn about patience. They interpret "don't say something strong to someone else out of anger" as "don't say something strong to someone out of a virtue." It's the same activity — saying something strong to someone, maybe sharply. Same activity, theoretically. Two different minds. You don't want to throw out the version that comes from a virtue. You want to throw out the version that comes from a delusion. So it's the same with this activity, thinking about the harm that's been done via delusions. We don't want to be doing that out of a delusion, which is a self-lacerating guilt, a depressed, discouraged guilt. I'm so horrible, I'm the worst. We don't want to do that, of course. That doesn't mean we shouldn't think about the harm that's been done, and have a sense of responsibility for that, and really see how the delusions make us do those things. That's a very useful activity.

So anyway, it's very, very useful to think about neglect that's been done. David, yes, thank you.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: So I think sometimes I have this issue of going into sort of self-judgment when I look at this kind of thing. And I realize, actually as you were saying that, I have a confusion about separating a delusion from ourself. Because it sounds like we have the control and responsibility right now to oppose the delusions. If we do that, we'll be free from them. So it's only because I haven't done that in the past that I still have this self-cherishing operating in my mind. So that feels like that is kind of my fault that I haven't already overcome my self-cherishing. And I'm wondering, is that view not distinguishing between myself and the delusion? Does that question make sense? And how can I parse that through?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Yeah, I know what you're saying — which is, okay, all the non-virtues that we've ever done come from the delusions. So therefore, it's the delusions' fault. But I haven't gotten rid of the delusions, so therefore, that's my fault. That's what you're saying, yeah.

What I would encourage is that there isn't a total clarity about the difference between ourself and our delusions, if that issue comes up. It's actually a very profound thing. It's not something we just say in Dharma classes — "we are not our delusions" — as a backup point to help people. It's not a throwaway point. It's a very, very profound thing that actually has to do with overcoming our self-grasping ignorance. I'll read a little bit from New Eight Steps in a second about this. But if we get it totally clear that we are not the delusions, we won't have this issue. That's the point.

As we know, there are these famous little sections — "living beings have no faults" and "looking at our faults in the mirror of Dharma" — and they both speak to this point in different ways.

[Reading from New Eight Steps to Happiness:] Geshe-la says here, for example, we normally refer to our body and mind as "my body" and "my mind," in a similar way to which we refer to our other possessions. This indicates that they are different from our I. The body and mind are the basis upon which we establish our I, not the I itself. Delusions are characteristics of a person's mind, not of the person.

What in the world does that mean? [Reading:] Since we can never find faults in sentient beings themselves, we can say that in this respect, sentient beings are like Buddhas.

Not a throwaway kind of point. Since we can never find faults in sentient beings themselves, we can say that in this respect, sentient beings are like Buddhas. So what we're trying to get the sense of is that this label I is just right now put on a body and mind, which are not the I at all. And all delusions are just characteristics of the mind that the I is placed upon. So all faults are coming from the delusions, not the I. I is just a label that has landed on these things. So when we become guilty or whatever, we're still thinking the I is those delusions. We're not actually relating to the I as just a label, like Jenny on a car, or Kyle, John, Mary, whatever, on the body and mind. We're still associating with the basis of imputation as the self.

So we need to sit with these points — not in a quick-and-dirty way, as an aside, but really as their own meditations, and get a visceral sense. To me, getting a visceral sense of this meditation is very similar to meditating on emptiness of the self, and realizing the emptiness of the self. It's not like, yeah, yeah, yeah, the delusions, whatever. I'm not saying that you're saying that — I'm just saying that's what I've done until I spent time with this point in more detail. I feel like I want to spend even more time on it personally. It basically is just like meditating on the emptiness of the self, if you think about it. When we meditate on the emptiness of the self, we try to think: I am not my mind. I am not my body. The mind is not the I. The body is not the I. There's no I separate from the body and mind. So one part of that entire meditation is thinking, the I is not the mind. It's a huge chunk of the meditation. So distinguishing between the delusions and the self is basically doing that part of the meditation. It's a huge part of the meditation, because most minds are pervaded by delusions all the time. So it's actually a very, very profound thing to do. And once we stop imputing our I on the delusions, then all these kinds of problems go away. It becomes a billion times easier to work on them also.

We know these sections, and we can read them in our own free time. But I would suggest, if we do that, don't read them quickly. Take like two lines, and chew them over a little bit. If you are quizzed precisely — "since we can never find faults in sentient beings themselves, we can say in this respect, sentient beings are like Buddhas" — if we are quizzed precisely, why exactly is that the case? In what sense? The point is, this is just so rich, and we should take a look when we get a chance to. Okay, thank you.

Faults of self-cherishing. We are going to be talking about this a little bit in the teaching skills next week. Everyone is invited, as always — 2:30 to 3:30. It's very nice when we approach meditation to think problem–solution as a couplet. Problem–solution. So here, the solution is offering our body, or basically opposing our self-cherishing. And what's really nice to do is to match it up with a personal problem that we want to solve. What's nice about that is that it makes us very interested in the solution.

So with the self-cherishing mind, we don't want to approach overcoming it by thinking, like, I'm supposed to overcome it, blah, blah, blah. The best way to do it is to think: what are my lived problems that I am freaking over with, that I want to go away? What are my real problems that I just despise, that I'm just done with, I'm fed up with? You know mine or yours? Anyway. So what we do is identify our lived problems that we are personally tired of — the things we're just so fed up with. And then all we have to do is link it to the solution. Fortunately, with overcoming self-cherishing, every single problem does link to it. Most delusions you can do this activity with pretty straightforwardly, and most practices you can do this with — the same exercise. But with self-cherishing it's particularly easy because every single problem on earth comes from self-cherishing. It's not a complicated practice. With prostrations, which is our next section, you can do this also — think of any problem in your life and how much you're just done with it, and you can conclude, prostrations is the answer. You can also do that with offerings.

So what we do is try to identify one of those problems for us. Make it personal, make it real. Make it something that we just absolutely despise and we're just done with, and we're fed up with. There's a ton that relate to self-cherishing. Taking ourselves too seriously — that's just a description of self-cherishing. So that's an annoying problem. We don't have to get all the problems. We just need one that we feel particularly motivated to be done with forever.

[Reading from New Eight Steps to Happiness:] It is because of self-cherishing that we take our wishes and plans so seriously and are unable to accept and learn from the difficulties that life brings us. He also says, all the problems of human society — such as war, crime, pollution, drug addiction, poverty, injustice, and disharmony within families — are the result of self-cherishing.

So if you hate any of those problems, great, you can blame self-cherishing. [Reading:] When people are unable to fulfill their wishes, many experience depression, discouragement, unhappiness, and mental pain, and some even want to kill themselves. This is because their self-cherishing believes that their wishes are so important.

Okay, those are big problems. Depression, discouragement, unhappiness, mental pain, suicidal thoughts. Those are really difficult, painful problems. They're all the fault of self-cherishing. [Reading:] Geshe-la says: anxiety, all disharmony, quarreling, and fighting comes from self-cherishing. All anger, all the times we've been miserable — we will discover they're characterized by an excessive concern for our own welfare. We lose things when we feel sad.

I'm not going to keep doing this, but you got the idea pretty quickly. I think we've covered all the problems of humankind.

So what we do — you get the sense of, like, I just really, really want to overcome this problem. I'm dying to overcome this problem. I'm done with it. Get this thing out of me. And then we just see, okay, how is that problem really the problem of self-cherishing? By thinking I am important while neglecting others, coming from the appearance of a true existence of a self. And then from that, we'll organically desire the solution. Okay, I want to offer my body, then. I want to break down the self-cherishing mind.

And the key here is that wish is the object of meditation. This is so important to get, both as Dharma teachers and as practitioners. Many people will then go to, well, then how do I do it, blah, blah, blah, but ignore the wish or the determination, which is the actual object of meditation. If we have the wish, everything else is easy. So we don't want to do this exercise and go, yeah, I want to overcome my self-cherishing, yeah, we know how to do it to some degree, we've already looked at a few things in the previous class, and then all the meditations on love and compassion and so on. That's the easy bit, actually — the tools that are just listed. The hard part is the wish. The wish is the hard part to get. A really powerful, clear wish that we meditate on, or a really powerful, clear determination that we meditate on. That's where we want to stop. In a sense, that's the antidote in and of itself, just the wish, the determination. When it becomes powerful enough, we will just naturally go for the solution and we'll do it so joyfully and happily. The point is just to simmer on that wish, that determination.

Just in conclusion of that point: we think of a real problem for us that we really are done with. We think about how much we despise that problem. We link it to self-cherishing — it might take a little bit of finagling, but we can probably get there if we think about it a little bit. Then through doing that, we just think, I want to overcome my self-cherishing — in brackets, so I can be free of this problem and a bunch of other problems too. Then we just try to sit with that determination. We don't run to the solution of getting rid of the self-cherishing mind. We don't run to the antidote. We just stop at the determination. It just takes a little bit of discipline to learn to do.

We probably can't keep lingering in this section. Does anyone have any questions about this specifically before we mosey? Ryan, yeah.

teaching.speaker: Ryan
teaching.text: I figured that uncontrolled desires, attachment, and lust is from self-cherishing. I just don't know how. Can you explain it quickly? And then what did you mean a minute ago when you said sit with it before running to the solution? Can you explain this?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
That second bit is straightforward — which is, the object of meditation that we're trying to reach is the wish to overcome the self-cherishing mind, or destroy it. The object of meditation isn't then some meditation on love, compassion, exchanging self with others, or whatever, that then opposes it. That's the next step. But if you don't stop at the wish and make it seared into the mind, what ends up happening is that we have a half-hearted interest, and we rush to a solution that we're trying to do with a half-hearted interest, and it doesn't land. If the wish is really, really powerful, any Dharma tool you grab will land like a ton of bricks. It'll hit really hard. When we try a Dharma practice and it doesn't work, it's simply because we don't really want to do it. We're just doing it because we're supposed to. We're going through the motions. Basically, it's a lack of wishing faith.

I know you often are wondering how can I remember to do this in a day. The answer is: get a bigger wish in the meditation. If you have a big wish in the meditation, you do something — you remember it. If we really, really want something, we just remember it. It's not hard to remember something we really, really want. If you have an amazing date with the person of your dreams at 9 p.m. tonight, are you going to forget? They're like your dream boat. There's no way you forget. You'll run over people to get there. You'll do anything to get there. So if we don't remember Dharma, it's mostly just because we don't want to actually remember it. So we just got to get a stronger wish. Okay, that's the wish part.

Then how to link desire-attachment to it. So all craving and desirous attachment comes because we think that we're important and we're neglecting others. We're usually not attached to things for others. Maybe some we're attached to, but for everyone else we're not bothered about whether they get this or get that. So whenever we're attached to something, it's because we're thinking very strongly: I'm important, and neglecting others. And then we think, I want the best for me. And I want it now. Basically the self-cherishing mind thinks: me, now. Those two thoughts. Me, now. We want whatever's good for us now, and we want whatever's bad for us out of the way now.

So you can do this exercise: just think, what am I attached to? I want this, I want this, I want this, I want that. Okay, how much do I think about wanting those things for other people? Like my random neighbor I see once in a while, and the person at the corner store. How much do I wish those things for them? Oh, like, never. Huh, that's interesting. So what's the difference? It's not that they don't know that those things are good or interesting. It's because I simply don't care about them. At all. So that means the interest, the attachment, is simply coming because I have too much care for the inherently existent self. That's the only reason that we're attached. So you just try to bridge the connection. That's just an example. Yeah, thanks Ryan.

So those are a lot of ways on offering our body. As we might know, in Vajrayogini practice we chop up our body and offer it as nectar. That's also very fun. In the Kusali tsog offering, you can read about that there. I remember when I first went to my first highest yoga tantra empowerment, we did that practice in the morning session at 7:30. And you're just sitting there, and everything up to that point has been very beautiful and elegant, and then the lyrics come: I chop up my flesh, body and bones, and heap it inside. Staring with wide open eyes, I purify, transform, and increase it into an ocean of nectar. I didn't even know about that! I chop up my flesh, body and bones, and heap it inside. Staring with wide open eyes, I purify and transform. Anyway, lovely practice. So you can do that too. That's another way to offer your body.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
Okay. Done. Offering our own body. Sublime offerings. I read out the in-between section in the meditation, so that's why we're skipping that now. Ordinary offerings — we just did in the meditation.

[Reading from Meaningful to Behold:] Sublime offerings are purer than the ordinary visualized offerings just made. They are offerings actually manifested by superior beings. In emulation of them, Shantideva prays: Just as Manjughosha and Samantabhadra made many beautiful offerings to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, similarly may I too make offerings to the protectors and their sons. Supreme beings such as Manjughosha and Samantabhadra have the ability, because of their spiritual realizations, to emanate such offerings as described above. At present we can only visualize such offerings, but superior Bodhisattvas — those advanced beings who possess both bodhichitta and direct insight into reality — are able to manifest such things and offer them to the enlightened beings for their use. Such manifestations can be used by ordinary sentient beings.

[Reading:] Powers of manifestation such as these were not unknown in India and Tibet. In One Hundred Thousand Songs of Milarepa, the story is told of the arrival in Tibet of the great Indian Pandit, Padampa Sangye. Milarepa wanted to test Padampa Sangye's spiritual powers, so he flew miraculously to a mountain near where the Indian was passing. As he awaited the arrival of the Pandit, Milarepa transformed himself into a flower near the roadside. When Padampa Sangye came by and walked past the flower, apparently unable to see through Milarepa's disguise, the Tibetan yogi thought the Indian had no powers of clairvoyance. How lame. Shortly after he thought this, however, the Pandit paused, turned around, and walked back to the flower. Kicking it sharply, he shouted, "You, Milarepa, stand up!" Milarepa immediately resumed his human form and greeted the Pandit warmly, saying, "Welcome to Tibet. You are indeed a great master."

Okay, so if you've never done this before, you're not there yet. If you've never noticed a sneaky little emanation and kicked it, said, Buddha, come on, come on out.

[Reading:] To this, Padampa Sangye replied, "You too are very famous in India as a great yogi." The story of the competition they then held to demonstrate each other's miracle powers, and the songs of realization Milarepa sang afterwards, can be read in several biographies which have already been translated into English.

So if you like reading stories, and you haven't read, for example, the biography of Milarepa and some of these other biographies, they're really worth reading. They're better than other stories, because they have a lot of spiritual benefit. You get blessings from reading them. So if you're not into stories or reading books, then it doesn't really matter. But if that's something you'd like to do, it's incredibly rich and beautiful to read the biographies of all the great yogis.

[Reading:] If we frequently make ordinary visualized offerings of the twelve types mentioned above, positive imprints will be placed in our minds that will eventually ripen our ability to make the sublime offerings of superior Bodhisattvas. However, there is another sublime offering that we can make right at this present moment, and that is to practice the teachings we have received from our spiritual guide or guru. If our spiritual guide gives us instructions on how to abandon non-virtue and practice virtue, and we follow these instructions faithfully, then this is a most sublime offering. Milarepa told his teacher Marpa that he had no material objects to offer him, but intended instead to repay his guru's kindness by dedicating his body, speech, and mind to the practice of Dharma. Because the spiritual guide is solely interested in the welfare of the disciples, such an offering of practice is much more pleasing to him than any amount of wealth. Another method of making sublime offerings is to transform whatever merit we may have collected from positive actions into gifts suitable for presentation to both enlightened and ordinary beings.

So the main point here is this practice of offering our practice. We've already talked about a little bit in our Reliance on a Spiritual Guide course that we had here. We talked about that a lot also there — that the principal way that we rely on a spiritual guide is in thought and in deed. In thought means viewing them as a Buddha. And then in deed means putting their teachings into practice as like an offering — but not doing things for them, not doing their laundry, or whatever. So of course just practicing Dharma is a sublime offering, but it's nice to then offer it also, overtly. It just makes it look even better.

So every time we do our meditation practice, we can just imagine offering that meditation to our guru. And just think they're so happy. It's the one thing the Buddhas can't do for us, right? They can't practice Dharma for us. Our mental continuum is causally related, and the cause of our previous moment of mind, or our current moment of mind, is the previous moment of mind, our karma. And the only things that will give rise to more moments of our mind are other things done with our own mind. It's a continuum of cause and effect. So our guru can't get into the continuum. He can't intervene in a continuum, because it's related to all of its previous moments. You can't just hop in halfway, because you'd have to be related to every single previous moment before that. As we know, there's this famous quote that Buddha can't take our suffering from us like a thorn from a foot. The one thing that our guru and the Buddhas can't do is practice Dharma for us. So when we do that, it is the best offering. It's the one thing they can't do for us. They can do everything else. They cannot do that. So it's an amazing offering. It's a very beautiful offering.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: When you say offering our practice, are we offering it before we do it, or are we offering the merit accumulated by doing it, or both? Is there a difference?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Traditionally, it's afterwards. You go, wow, that was amazing. You rejoice in it, and you say, here Buddha, I was just patient with that person, or I didn't attack them, or whatever. I let them go first in line.

teaching.speaker: Fran
teaching.text: So it's not just a seated practice — it's anything?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text:
No, it's principally in daily life. It's a really, really powerful thing to do. It just takes the virtue we're creating anyway, makes us notice it and celebrate it, and then makes it increase by making it an offering, a gift. And the Buddhas are just so happy. They're so happy for us. It's a thing that they've been trying to get us to do for billions of eons, and we've stubbornly refused. So when we're finally doing that, they just can't believe it. Wow, they're doing it. Yes. I'm so happy for them. It's such an exciting thing. They watch us struggle for billions of lives, and toil, and mess up. It's like a parent with their kid who keeps messing up over and over again. And you just — you'll do it one day. But this is like a billions-and-billions-of-lives version. So when we're practicing — what a delight. Just crying of joy watching us practice. Just trying, just showing up. Amazing.

Okay, that's good. So the main thing is offering our body equals overcoming self-cherishing, especially imputing I on an ordinary suffering body and mind. And we looked at lots of little ways to do that. So let's make sure that our practice in the break is focused on that. But we can use any of the methods that we talked about as we'd like.

Okay, let's have a little time for discussion. We've got a nice gaggle in here today — ten people. We're just going to do this somewhat geographically. Mary Ann and David. Anne P. and Mimi. Ryan and Neil. Fran and Suzanne. And Jose and Anne. Okay, thank you.

conclusion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
conclusion.text:
All right everyone, thank you. Anyone have anything you'd like to share before we wrap it up? Offer our body? Overcome our self-cherishing? Anything else we want to do? That's it, right?

Okay. Oh, make our list. Our neglect list. Yeah. Put it on the wall, baby. I think we should all just have our neglect lists on the wall in the basement. So we can all look at it. You can write the name and then the main grievance, the main damage. If you can't think of something, you have missed the boat on that one. Because by not being a Buddha, we're neglecting all living beings every day. Strangers, exactly — all the people suffering in the hells and all the animals and hungry ghosts and so on that we can't help because we're busy doing other stuff. And then you can at least think of countless past lives too where there was some hearty neglect in there. All because of dumb old self-cherishing.

Any last bits? Greetings, online folk. You're in a different place today. Oh, very nice. Different lighting. You're on a couch with a kitty.

Okay. Just a reminder, we have our Vajradaka Burning Offering Bonanza next Saturday the 18th. It's also a course on Living in the Present that day. Good topic. And then the U.S. Festival coming soon. And then Walk for World Peace. Put it on your radar, please. It is the 17th of May. It's a really important community event. So I hope you can be there. Dogs welcome. Partners welcome. In-laws welcome. The whole bunch. Your Maras are welcome. Yeah, you can leave them home if you want. But they're also welcome if you really want to bring them. But it's a beautiful day, so please do join in the fun if you can.

Okay, we can just dedicate now. We can think — the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal dedications or prayers.

Okay, very nice. Thank you, everyone. Just one nice little object of rejoicing. When we had our empowerment, we had a lot of people come from different centers, including from the temple and from KMC New York City. And I've now been told by five different people that they were very touched by the kind and joyful and harmonious energy and behavior of everyone here. To the point where they went out of their way to tell me. And even one person told me because someone else told them, because they were so moved. Someone who has been a longtime practitioner — she came here and she was very moved by the harmony and peace and joy. She was raving about that to someone else who then told me secondhand. So about five different people who gave that feedback. And I thought that was very touching. And it's such a good example that we're setting. And it's a very nice offering to others too — other practitioners and people — to demonstrate a very joyful, happy, pure example like that. I thought that was just so lovely. I just wanted to make sure that you knew that that was what I heard on the street from other people. Which is amazing. Okay, thank you so much. Thank you.
